hints: Focus on writing the full electron configuration for each atom and ion, remembering to remove 4s electrons before 3d electrons for transition metal ions.
Start with the simple cases, calcium is $\text{Ca}$ $[\text{Ar}]4s^2$ with zero unpaired electrons and aluminium is $\text{Al}$ $[\text{Ne}]3s^2 3p^1$ with one unpaired electron.
Now count unpaired electrons in the 3d subshell for $\text{Cu}^{2+}$, $\text{Cr}^{3+}$, $\text{Ni}^{2+}$ and $\text{Fe}^{3+}$, then match the pair with equal counts.
walkthrough:
**Recall how to count unpaired electrons**

Unpaired electrons are electrons that sit alone in an orbital. For s and p subshells this is simple, and for d subshells we fill each of the five d orbitals singly before pairing.

Rule for ions:
$$\text{remove } 4s \text{ electrons before } 3d \text{ electrons}$$

**Work out the s and p block species**

Aluminium is atomic number 13: $[\text{Ne}]3s^2 3p^1$, so the single 3p electron is unpaired, giving 1.

Calcium is atomic number 20: $[\text{Ar}]4s^2$, fully paired, giving 0.

Oxide ion, $\text{O}^{2-}$, is $1s^2 2s^2 2p^6$, a full noble gas octet, giving 0.

**Work out the transition metal ions**

Copper is $[\text{Ar}]3d^{10}4s^1$, so $\text{Cu}^{2+}$ loses the 4s then one 3d: $[\text{Ar}]3d^9$, giving 1 unpaired.

Chromium is $[\text{Ar}]3d^5 4s^1$, so $\text{Cr}^{3+}$ is $[\text{Ar}]3d^3$, giving 3 unpaired.

Nickel is $[\text{Ar}]3d^8 4s^2$, so $\text{Ni}^{2+}$ is $[\text{Ar}]3d^8$, giving 2 unpaired.

Iron is $[\text{Ar}]3d^6 4s^2$, so $\text{Fe}^{3+}$ is $[\text{Ar}]3d^5$, giving 5 unpaired.

**Match the pairs**

Only aluminium (1) and $\text{Cu}^{2+}$ (1) have the same number. All other pairs are 0 vs 3, 0 vs 2, and 5 vs 0.

options.A: Al is $[Ne]3s^2 3p^1$ with 1 unpaired electron. Cu is $[Ar]3d^{10}4s^1$, so Cu2+ is $[Ar]3d^9$ with 1 unpaired electron. Both have one, so this pair matches.
options.B: Ca is $[Ar]4s^2$ with 0 unpaired electrons (diamagnetic). Cr3+ is $[Ar]3d^3$ with 3 unpaired electrons. Students who forget Ca has a full 4s pair or miscount Cr3+ often pick this.
options.C: Ca has 0 unpaired electrons, while Ni2+ is $[Ar]3d^8$ with 2 unpaired electrons. This is a common trap if you think Ni2+ loses 3d electrons instead of 4s electrons.
options.D: Fe3+ is $[Ar]3d^5$ with 5 unpaired electrons (half-filled d subshell, maximum). O2- is $1s^2 2s^2 2p^6$ with 0 unpaired electrons. They do not match.
